- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥ 0.6) over recent days, model tends to under-forecast; adjust upward by 1–2% of recent mean or 0.5–1.0 price point.
- When sentiment is negative (≤ -0.4), model often over-anticipates recovery; reduce forecast by 0.5–1.5 price points to avoid overshoot.
- After a sharp price spike (≥ 3% from prior peak), model frequently overreacts and forecasts continued ascent; cap forecast at 1–2 price points below true peak or apply lagged mean reversion.
- If sentiment shifts from negative to positive within 5–7 days, model often fails to adjust quickly; apply a 3–5 day smoothing filter or delay forecast rise by 1–2 days.
- For 30-day horizon, model consistently underestimates upward momentum in bullish sentiment; add 0.5–1.5 price point bias toward higher end of forecast range if sentiment > 0.6.
- If sentiment is neutral or mixed (0.2–0.6), model often over-optimistically forecasts upward trend; apply 0.5–1.0 price point downward correction to avoid false breakout.
- When sentiment is volatile (rapid swings), model tends to overfit short-term noise; use 3–5 day moving average or sentiment-weighted smoothing to dampen erratic forecasts.
